screens.title: Advanced Troubleshooting of Connection & Authentication
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we take a structured approach to the most disruptive class of operational incidents: connection and authentication failures. You will learn to work from client to server, validating network reachability, port accessibility, firewall and DNS behavior, and then inspect server-side configuration such as listen_addresses, pg_hba. conf ordering, and resource limits like max_connections. I’ll show concrete commands you can use to separate a network problem from an authentication problem, and how to spot idle in transaction sessions that silently exhaust connection slots. We’ll also practice using tools like pg_isready and psql options that bypass DNS to isolate issues. These skills matter because when connections fail the database appears down even if it is healthy, and a quick, methodical diagnosis minimizes downtime. As you move through the screens, consider how the same stepwise checklist reduces guesswork and avoids making risky changes. Think: what would you check first if an application suddenly reported connection refused?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Overview
Advanced Troubleshooting of Connection & Authentication
A practical checklist to isolate network, authentication, and server-side limits that block clients from connecting.
In this lesson

Learn commands, config checks, and diagnostic techniques to restore connectivity quickly and safely.

Why it matters

Connection failures make the database unreachable; a repeatable process reduces downtime and prevents misconfiguration cascading into outages.

Explore Key Topics
pg_hba.conf
Order and methods determine who can authenticate and how; reload after edits.
Network & Firewall
Test port reachability with telnet or netcat and verify listen_addresses and security groups.
Resource Limits
Monitor max_connections and idle in transaction sessions via pg_stat_activity.
This visual shows the simple chain we will test: client reachability, network/firewall pass-through, and server configuration. Each step can block connections, and we'll practice commands that isolate the failing layer.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to run a repeatable diagnostic checklist that separates network reachability from authentication and resource issues. You will learn to inspect pg_hba. conf entries, understand how rule order affects authentication, and reliably reload configuration changes. You will also be able to test ports with telnet or netcat, use pg_isready to determine server responsiveness, and apply psql options like hostaddr and sslmode to narrow DNS or TLS issues. Finally, you will recognize when max_connections or idle in transaction sessions are causing failures and apply targeted fixes such as terminating backends or increasing limits. Each objective pairs a practical command or query with the reasoning behind it so you can explain your remediation steps to application teams and reduce repeated incidents. screens.title: Practical checks and remediation steps
screens.narratorSegment: In addition to diagnostic reasoning, you will practice exact remediation steps: how to update pg_hba. conf safely, the correct way to reload PostgreSQL so new rules take effect, and when a restart is required. You will also learn to update firewall rules and verify them, and use psql with hostaddr to avoid DNS ambiguity. Finally, we cover secure connection management strategies such as preferring scram-sha-256 or md5 consistently in pg_hba. conf and documenting allowed client networks so future edits do not regress access. These hands-on actions reduce incident repeatability and keep your posture secure. For each remediation you will practice a quick verification step that ensures the change achieved the intended result without collateral risk. Keep a log of changes and always reload rather than restart when you only modify authentication or HBA rules.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Practical Checks
Four remediation tasks
A. Edit pg_hba.conf
Add or reorder rules, set methods to md5 or scram-sha-256, then reload to apply.
B. Adjust firewall
Open inbound port 5432 for allowed networks or remove accidental DROP rules, then retest connectivity.
C. Fix listen_addresses
Set listen_addresses to an interface IP or '*' for remote clients and reload or restart when required.
D. Free connections
Identify idle in transaction sessions and terminate backends or increase max_connections with restart if safe.
Verification steps
  • Use pg_isready to confirm server responds without auth.
  • Telnet or netcat to confirm port reachability.
  • Attempt a psql connection using hostaddr to bypass DNS.

screens.title: A repeatable troubleshooting checklist
screens.narratorSegment: A disciplined checklist prevents wasted effort when solving connection problems. Start by confirming the server process is running; on Debian-style systems check the unit status, which tells you if PostgreSQL is active. Next, verify the server is listening on the expected port and interface using netstat or ss; a listen on 127.0.0.1 restricts access to local clients only. Then confirm network reachability from the client: ping can validate IP-level connectivity, but telnet or netcat against the database port shows whether the port is reachable and accepting TCP connections. If the port is blocked, inspect firewall settings and cloud security groups. If the port is reachable but authentication fails, inspect pg_hba. conf for matching rules, paying attention to rule order and the specified authentication method. After making changes to pg_hba. conf or postgresql. conf (other than listen_addresses), reload the server configuration instead of restarting to avoid unnecessary downtime. Finally, check server resources and connections with pg_stat_activity to ensure you are not hitting max_connections or leaking idle in transaction sessions. This sequence—from running service, listening socket, network, authentication, to resources—lets you isolate the failing layer quickly.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Checklist
Step-by-step diagnostic flow
1. Is PostgreSQL running?
Check the service status and recent logs to rule out a crashed server.
2. Is it listening where you expect?
Use netstat or ss to confirm listen_addresses and port presence.
3. Can the client reach the port?
Use telnet or nc to validate TCP-level access; if failing, check firewalls and security groups.
4. Is authentication allowed?
Inspect pg_hba.conf rules and ordering; verify matching host, user, db and method.
5. Are there free connection slots?
Query pg_stat_activity and compare to max_connections to decide if you need to free or increase slots.
Commands to know
sudo systemctl status postgresql@12-main
sudo netstat -tulpn | grep 5432
telnet <server_ip> 5432  # or nc -vz <server_ip> 5432
pg_isready -h <host> -p 5432 -d <db> -U <user>
psql -h <server_ip> -p 5432 -U <user> -d <db>
Key Takeaway

A consistent checklist reduces time to resolution: verify process, listening, network, HBA, then resources.

screens.title: pg_hba.conf essentials
screens.narratorSegment: The pg_hba. conf file is PostgreSQL’s host-based authentication policy. It lists rules that match a client by address, user, database, and method, and PostgreSQL applies the first rule that matches. That order is the most common source of confusion: a restrictive rule placed above a permissive one will prevent a later match from ever being considered. For example, a top-line reject for all hosts will block any later specific allow. Common authentication methods include trust, md5, and scram-sha-256; using the wrong method for your client will cause authentication to fail even if the network and user mapping are correct. After editing pg_hba. conf you must reload the configuration to apply changes. When debugging, explicitly verify the matching rule and ensure IP ranges and netmasks are correct. A frequent misconception is thinking a permissive rule lower in the file will override an earlier reject; it will not. Always check the first matching line and, if necessary, temporarily add a specific allow entry above a broad reject to test access before committing changes. pg_hba.conf essentials means rules are evaluated top to bottom; the first matching rule determines whether a client can authenticate and by which method.. In practical terms, how rules, order, and authentication methods determine access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › pg_hba.conf
What to check in pg_hba.conf
  • Correct host/netmask for the client IP range.
  • User and database fields match the incoming connection.
  • Authentication method is appropriate for the client (md5 vs scram-sha-256).
  • Rule order: the first match wins.
Concrete example
# problematic order - reject before allow
host all all 0.0.0.0/0 reject
host all myuser 192.168.1.0/24 md5

# correct order
host all myuser 192.168.1.0/24 md5
host all all 0.0.0.0/0 reject
Troubleshooting tips
  1. Search logs for "no pg_hba.conf entry" messages to see which host and user were rejected.
  2. Temporarily add a narrow allow rule above broad rejects to test connectivity safely.
  3. Reload the server after edits instead of restarting when possible.
Common mistake

Placing a broad reject too early, assuming a later allow will fix access, and forgetting to reload after edits.

screens.title: Authentication methods and common mismatches
screens.narratorSegment: Authentication methods determine how PostgreSQL verifies credentials. The trust method allows a connection without a password for a matching host, which can be useful for controlled local environments but is insecure for remote access. Password-based methods such as md5 and scram-sha-256 require correct credentials; scram-sha-256 is a more modern and secure hashing mechanism. A frequent source of failure is a mismatch between the client expectation and the configured method: a client trying to authenticate with a password will fail if the rule uses trust, and a client that cannot handle scram will fail if the server requires it. When deciding which method to use, prefer a consistent password method for remote clients and reserve trust for tightly controlled local connections. Also verify that usernames and database names are spelled and cased correctly, because PostgreSQL treats identifiers as case-sensitive when quoted. Remember that changing authentication methods requires a configuration reload. When troubleshooting an authentication failure, check logs for messages like password authentication failed and confirm the effective pg_hba. conf rule. Authentication methods and common mismatches means ensure the authentication method in pg_hba.conf matches client capabilities and that usernames are exact; mismatches cause rejection even when reachability is fine.. In practical terms, trust, md5, scram-sha-256 — choosing the right method. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Auth Methods
Method comparison
trust
Allows connection without a password when matched. Use only for local, controlled environments.
md5
Password-based authentication using MD5 hash. Widely supported by clients.
scram-sha-256
More secure password hashing. Prefer for modern deployments if clients support it.
Misconfiguration example
If pg_hba.conf contains 'trust' for a client but the team expects password auth, connections succeed without passwords when allowed, or if they send a password the server may still accept but this creates security risk. Conversely, if the server requires scram-sha-256 and the client only supports md5, authentication fails.
Checks and fixes
  • Confirm client capability for scram or md5.
  • Match auth method in pg_hba.conf to client requirements.
  • Reload config and retest; watch for log messages describing failed auth attempts.

screens.title: Network reachability and firewall diagnostics
screens.narratorSegment: Network reachability issues are the most frequent cause of apparent database unavailability. Begin by confirming basic IP reachability with ping, but remember ping only checks ICMP. The decisive tests for a database port are telnet or netcat: attempting a TCP handshake to the server IP and port shows whether the port is reachable and has an active listener. If these fail, the culprit is commonly a firewall on the client, server, or a cloud security group between them. Check server-side firewall tools like ufw, firewalld, or iptables and cloud network rules to ensure inbound 5432 is allowed. Also verify listen_addresses; even if the firewall is open, PostgreSQL may only be listening on localhost. DNS problems can mask network issues; use psql hostaddr or connect by IP to bypass DNS while testing. A common mistake is changing pg_hba. conf before confirming port reachability — that wastes time because authentication will never be attempted if the connection cannot be established. By validating reachability first, you separate firewall or routing issues from authentication configuration problems. Network reachability and firewall diagnostics means always verify tcp reachability to the database port before editing server authentication; telnet or nc will tell you if the port responds.. In practical terms, use simple tcp checks to find blocking firewalls or wrong interfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Network Diagnostics
Connectivity tests
ping <server_ip_or_hostname>
# TCP check
telnet <server_ip> 5432
nc -vz <server_ip> 5432
# Bypass DNS in psql
psql -h <server_ip> -p 5432 -U <user> -d <db>  # use hostaddr variant if needed
If telnet or nc shows connection refused or no route to host, focus on firewall and network routing. If TCP connects but authentication fails, move on to pg_hba.conf checks.
Firewall checklist
  • Check ufw status or iptables rules on the server.
  • If in cloud, verify security groups or network ACLs allow inbound 5432 from the client.
  • Temporarily allow port 5432 and retest; revert test rules afterward.
Common mistake

Assuming the database listens on all interfaces when listen_addresses is left at localhost.

screens.title: listen_addresses and interface binding
screens.narratorSegment: The listen_addresses setting in postgresql. conf controls which network interfaces PostgreSQL binds to. A value of localhost or 127.0.0.1 restricts connections to the host itself, which is safe for single-node local testing but prevents any remote client from connecting. For remote access set listen_addresses to '*' or a specific interface IP; changes to listen_addresses generally require a server restart rather than a simple reload. A common diagnostic is to run netstat or ss to confirm where the server socket is bound — you should see 0.0.0.0:5432 or a specific IP rather than 127.0.0.1:5432 if remote clients must connect. Remember that even with listen_addresses configured correctly, you still need matching pg_hba. conf entries and firewall rules permitting the traffic. A typical mistake is toggling pg_hba. conf to allow remote hosts while forgetting to update listen_addresses, causing puzzling behavior where the HBA would look correct but connections are refused. Verify all three: listening socket, firewall, and HBA to restore remote connectivity. listen_addresses and interface binding means listen_addresses controls interface binding; ensure it's set to the required interfaces and restart if you change it.. In practical terms, why postgresql may accept local but not remote connections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › listen_addresses
Confirm where PostgreSQL is listening
# Check listen_addresses via server
sudo netstat -tulpn | grep 5432
# In psql
SHOW listen_addresses;
SHOW port;
Look for 127.0.0.1:5432 (local only) vs 0.0.0.0:5432 (all interfaces). If you change listen_addresses to allow remote access, plan for a restart if required by your distribution or version.
Checklist before allowing remote clients
  • Set listen_addresses to '*' or the server IP.
  • Open firewall ports and verify network reachability.
  • Add specific pg_hba.conf rules for allowed client IPs and methods.
Pro tip

Prefer explicit interface IPs in production rather than '*' when possible, then document the change.

screens.title: pg_isready and psql connection options
screens.narratorSegment: pg_isready is a minimal, non-authenticating probe that checks whether a server is accepting connections. It returns discrete codes to help interpret the result: success, no response, invalid connection string, and unavailable server. Use it when you need a fast answer about responsiveness without providing credentials. For more specific tests with psql, use hostaddr to connect by IP rather than hostname to bypass DNS resolution and sslmode to force or disable TLS negotiations during diagnosis. Together these options let you separate DNS failures from TLS or auth failures. For example, if pg_isready shows the server is accepting connections but psql fails when using a hostname, test with hostaddr pointing at the server; if that succeeds, a DNS issue is likely. If psql still fails and the server responds, inspect pg_hba. conf for method mismatches and check logs for password authentication failed messages. Using these targeted flags reduces the likelihood of making changes that don’t address the real problem. pg_isready and psql connection options means pg_isready and psql flags like hostaddr and sslmode let you separate dns, tls, and authentication issues efficiently.. In practical terms, use lightweight checks and targeted psql options to isolate dns and tls issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Client Tools
pg_isready usage
pg_isready -h <host> -p 5432 -d <db> -U <user>
# Exit codes: 0=accepting, 1=no response, 2=invalid conn string, 3=unavailable
Use pg_isready when you want a quick liveness check without credentials. It’s often the first tool to run in automation and monitoring checks.
psql flags to isolate problems
# Connect by IP to bypass DNS
psql -h <server_ip> -p 5432 -U <user> -d <db>
# Force TLS modes
psql "host=<host> port=5432 dbname=<db> user=<user> sslmode=disable"
If hostaddr connection succeeds but hostname fails, investigate DNS. If disabling sslmode allows auth, review TLS configuration and client certificates.

screens.title: max_connections and idle_in_transaction
screens.narratorSegment: max_connections sets the cap on concurrent client sessions. When this value is reached new connections are rejected with messages explaining that connection slots are reserved or that there are too many clients. Before increasing max_connections, inspect current usage: run SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity to see the active count and examine pg_stat_activity for state values. An especially harmful state is idle in transaction: a client has begun a transaction and then stopped issuing work without committing or rolling back, holding locks and consuming a slot. To find these, query pg_stat_activity for state = 'idle in transaction' and identify pid, user, and query_start. You can terminate problematic sessions using SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid);. Increasing max_connections requires a restart and can increase memory use per connection, so terminating idle sessions or adjusting application behavior to avoid long transactions is often the safer first step. A common misconception is to raise max_connections immediately; this can mask inefficient client behavior and lead to heavier resource usage. Fix the root cause where possible. max_connections and idle_in_transaction means prefer terminating idle in transaction sessions or fixing application behavior over only increasing max_connections; increasing requires restart and impacts resources.. In practical terms, detect and remediate connection exhaustion and stalled sessions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Queries to inspect connections

SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity;

-- Find idle in transaction sessions
SELECT pid, usename, datname, state, query_start, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction';

Use these queries to identify problematic sessions and terminate them when safe. Document and coordinate with app teams before killing connections in production.
When to increase max_connections

screens.title: Using PostgreSQL logs to pinpoint errors
screens.narratorSegment: PostgreSQL logs are the most direct source of truth when diagnosing authentication and connection errors. Look for messages such as "no pg_hba. conf entry for host" which indicates an HBA mismatch, or "password authentication failed for user" which indicates credential or method mismatch. If you see socket errors or connection refused entries, the problem is usually at the network or listen layer. Always correlate the timestamp in the log with the failed client attempt so you inspect the right event. Logs can also show when the server is overloaded or when autovacuum or background processes are failing, which can indirectly affect connections. When logs are sparse, increase client_min_messages or log_connections temporarily to capture more detail during investigation. A common mistaken approach is to change multiple settings at once; instead, make one change, reload or restart as required, and reproduce the failure to see the log entry that confirms the effect. That single-change approach reduces the risk of masking the root cause. Using PostgreSQL logs to pinpoint errors means match log messages and timestamps to client errors to identify whether the failure is network, authentication, or resource-related.. In practical terms, read log snippets and match them to the failing layer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Scenario: Client cannot connect
You are provided: telnet fails, listen_addresses shows 0.0.0.0, pg_hba.conf includes an allow for the client. What is the likely cause and the minimal fix?

screens.title: Safe change and verification timeline
screens.narratorSegment: When you must change configuration to restore access, follow a conservative timeline: first record the current state and capture logs so you can undo changes if needed. Next, apply the smallest change that targets the identified root cause — for example add a single pg_hba. conf allow for a specific client IP above broader rules, or open a firewall rule only for that address. After making the change, reload PostgreSQL when the edit is to pg_hba. conf or postgresql. conf settings that support reload; reserve restarts for listen_addresses changes or kernel-level adjustments. Then verify using pg_isready, telnet or nc, and a psql connection. Observe logs for new entries to confirm the server accepted the change. If the change resolved the issue, document the action, rationale, and verification steps so future incidents are faster to diagnose. If not, revert and proceed to the next hypothesis in your checklist. This careful timeline avoids cascading changes and reduces the chance of introducing new problems while troubleshooting. Safe change and verification timeline means apply minimal targeted changes, prefer reloads over restarts when possible, and always verify with concrete connection tests and logs.. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we take a structured approach to the most disruptive class of operational incidents: connection and authentication failures. You will learn to work from client to server, validating network reachability, port accessibility, firewall and DNS behavior, and then inspect server-side configuration such as listen_addresses, pg_hba. conf ordering, and resource limits like max_connections. I’ll show concrete commands you can use to separate a network problem from an authentication problem, and how to spot idle in transaction sessions that silently exhaust connection slots. We’ll also practice using tools like pg_isready and psql options that bypass DNS to isolate issues. These skills matter because when connections fail the database appears down even if it is healthy, and a quick, methodical diagnosis minimizes downtime. As you move through the screens, consider how the same stepwise checklist reduces guesswork and avoids making risky changes. Think: what would you check first if an application suddenly reported connection refused?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to run a repeatable diagnostic checklist that separates network reachability from authentication and resource issues. You will learn to inspect pg_hba. conf entries, understand how rule order affects authentication, and reliably reload configuration changes. You will also be able to test ports with telnet or netcat, use pg_isready to determine server responsiveness, and apply psql options like hostaddr and sslmode to narrow DNS or TLS issues. Finally, you will recognize when max_connections or idle in transaction sessions are causing failures and apply targeted fixes such as terminating backends or increasing limits. Each objective pairs a practical command or query with the reasoning behind it so you can explain your remediation steps to application teams and reduce repeated incidents. Learning Objectives means a methodical troubleshooting workflow that uses simple tools and queries to find the root cause of connection failures and fix them safely.. In practical terms, skills you will practice and verify. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

In addition to diagnostic reasoning, you will practice exact remediation steps: how to update pg_hba. conf safely, the correct way to reload PostgreSQL so new rules take effect, and when a restart is required. You will also learn to update firewall rules and verify them, and use psql with hostaddr to avoid DNS ambiguity. Finally, we cover secure connection management strategies such as preferring scram-sha-256 or md5 consistently in pg_hba. conf and documenting allowed client networks so future edits do not regress access. These hands-on actions reduce incident repeatability and keep your posture secure. For each remediation you will practice a quick verification step that ensures the change achieved the intended result without collateral risk. Keep a log of changes and always reload rather than restart when you only modify authentication or HBA rules.

A disciplined checklist prevents wasted effort when solving connection problems. Start by confirming the server process is running; on Debian-style systems check the unit status, which tells you if PostgreSQL is active. Next, verify the server is listening on the expected port and interface using netstat or ss; a listen on 127.0.0.1 restricts access to local clients only. Then confirm network reachability from the client: ping can validate IP-level connectivity, but telnet or netcat against the database port shows whether the port is reachable and accepting TCP connections. If the port is blocked, inspect firewall settings and cloud security groups. If the port is reachable but authentication fails, inspect pg_hba. conf for matching rules, paying attention to rule order and the specified authentication method. After making changes to pg_hba. conf or postgresql. conf (other than listen_addresses), reload the server configuration instead of restarting to avoid unnecessary downtime. Finally, check server resources and connections with pg_stat_activity to ensure you are not hitting max_connections or leaking idle in transaction sessions. This sequence—from running service, listening socket, network, authentication, to resources—lets you isolate the failing layer quickly.

The pg_hba. conf file is PostgreSQL’s host-based authentication policy. It lists rules that match a client by address, user, database, and method, and PostgreSQL applies the first rule that matches. That order is the most common source of confusion: a restrictive rule placed above a permissive one will prevent a later match from ever being considered. For example, a top-line reject for all hosts will block any later specific allow. Common authentication methods include trust, md5, and scram-sha-256; using the wrong method for your client will cause authentication to fail even if the network and user mapping are correct. After editing pg_hba. conf you must reload the configuration to apply changes. When debugging, explicitly verify the matching rule and ensure IP ranges and netmasks are correct. A frequent misconception is thinking a permissive rule lower in the file will override an earlier reject; it will not. Always check the first matching line and, if necessary, temporarily add a specific allow entry above a broad reject to test access before committing changes. pg_hba.conf essentials means rules are evaluated top to bottom; the first matching rule determines whether a client can authenticate and by which method.. In practical terms, how rules, order, and authentication methods determine access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Authentication methods determine how PostgreSQL verifies credentials. The trust method allows a connection without a password for a matching host, which can be useful for controlled local environments but is insecure for remote access. Password-based methods such as md5 and scram-sha-256 require correct credentials; scram-sha-256 is a more modern and secure hashing mechanism. A frequent source of failure is a mismatch between the client expectation and the configured method: a client trying to authenticate with a password will fail if the rule uses trust, and a client that cannot handle scram will fail if the server requires it. When deciding which method to use, prefer a consistent password method for remote clients and reserve trust for tightly controlled local connections. Also verify that usernames and database names are spelled and cased correctly, because PostgreSQL treats identifiers as case-sensitive when quoted. Remember that changing authentication methods requires a configuration reload. When troubleshooting an authentication failure, check logs for messages like password authentication failed and confirm the effective pg_hba. conf rule. Authentication methods and common mismatches means ensure the authentication method in pg_hba.conf matches client capabilities and that usernames are exact; mismatches cause rejection even when reachability is fine.. In practical terms, trust, md5, scram-sha-256 — choosing the right method. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Network reachability issues are the most frequent cause of apparent database unavailability. Begin by confirming basic IP reachability with ping, but remember ping only checks ICMP. The decisive tests for a database port are telnet or netcat: attempting a TCP handshake to the server IP and port shows whether the port is reachable and has an active listener. If these fail, the culprit is commonly a firewall on the client, server, or a cloud security group between them. Check server-side firewall tools like ufw, firewalld, or iptables and cloud network rules to ensure inbound 5432 is allowed. Also verify listen_addresses; even if the firewall is open, PostgreSQL may only be listening on localhost. DNS problems can mask network issues; use psql hostaddr or connect by IP to bypass DNS while testing. A common mistake is changing pg_hba. conf before confirming port reachability — that wastes time because authentication will never be attempted if the connection cannot be established. By validating reachability first, you separate firewall or routing issues from authentication configuration problems. Network reachability and firewall diagnostics means always verify tcp reachability to the database port before editing server authentication; telnet or nc will tell you if the port responds.. In practical terms, use simple tcp checks to find blocking firewalls or wrong interfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The listen_addresses setting in postgresql. conf controls which network interfaces PostgreSQL binds to. A value of localhost or 127.0.0.1 restricts connections to the host itself, which is safe for single-node local testing but prevents any remote client from connecting. For remote access set listen_addresses to '*' or a specific interface IP; changes to listen_addresses generally require a server restart rather than a simple reload. A common diagnostic is to run netstat or ss to confirm where the server socket is bound — you should see 0.0.0.0:5432 or a specific IP rather than 127.0.0.1:5432 if remote clients must connect. Remember that even with listen_addresses configured correctly, you still need matching pg_hba. conf entries and firewall rules permitting the traffic. max_connections sets the cap on concurrent client sessions. When this value is reached new connections are rejected with messages explaining that connection slots are reserved or that there are too many clients. Before increasing max_connections, inspect current usage: run SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity to see the active count and examine pg_stat_activity for state values. An especially harmful state is idle in transaction: a client has begun a transaction and then stopped issuing work without committing or rolling back, holding locks and consuming a slot. To find these, query pg_stat_activity for state = 'idle in transaction' and identify pid, user, and query_start. You can terminate problematic sessions using SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid);.
